Proof:
Let $n \in \N_{>0}$.
We aim to show that $\AA_n$ is a [[Definition:Discrete Set of Subsets|discrete set of subsets]].
To achieve this, we will demonstrate that for any $z \in X$, the set $\map {V_{n+2}} z = \set {y \in X : \tuple {z, y} \in V_{n+2}}$ intersects at most one element of $\AA_n$.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there exists a point $z \in X$ such that $\map {V_{n+2}} z$ intersects two distinct elements of $\AA_n$.
Since $\preccurlyeq$ is a well-ordering, it is a total ordering, so we can denote these two elements as $\map {A_n} {x_1}$ and $\map {A_n} {x_2}$ with $x_1 \preccurlyeq x_2$ and $x_1 \ne x_2$.
Let $y_1 \in \map {V_{n+2}} z \cap \map {A_n} {x_1}$ and $y_2 \in \map {V_{n+2}} z \cap \map {A_n} {x_2}$.

Since $y_1 \in \map {V_{n+2}} z$ and $y_2 \in \map {V_{n+2}} z$, we have $\tuple {z, y_1} \in V_{n+2}$ and $\tuple {z, y_2} \in V_{n+2}$.
Because $V_{n+2}$ is a symmetric relation, we have $\tuple {y_1, z} \in V_{n+2}$.
By the definition of composite relation, since $\tuple {y_1, z} \in V_{n+2}$ and $\tuple {z, y_2} \in V_{n+2}$, it follows that $\tuple {y_1, y_2} \in V_{n+2} \circ V_{n+2}$.
By hypothesis, $V_{n+2} \circ V_{n+2} \subseteq V_{n+1}$, which implies $\tuple {y_1, y_2} \in V_{n+1}$.

Since $y_1 \in \map {A_n} {x_1}$ and $\map {A_n} {x_1} \subseteq \map {U_n} {x_1}$, we have $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \in U_n$.
Therefore, since $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \in U_n$ and $\tuple {y_1, y_2} \in V_{n+1}$, by the definition of composite relation, we have $\tuple {x_1, y_2} \in V_{n+1} \circ U_n$.
By the definition of $U_{n+1}$, we have $V_{n+1} \circ U_n = V_{n+1} \circ V_n \circ \cdots \circ V_1 = U_{n+1}$.
Thus, $\tuple {x_1, y_2} \in U_{n+1}$, which means $y_2 \in \map {U_{n+1}} {x_1}$.

However, $y_2 \in \map {A_n} {x_2}$, and by definition:
$\map {A_n} {x_2} = \map {U_n} {x_2} \setminus \ds \bigcup_{y \preccurlyeq x_2, y \ne x_2} \map {U_{n + 1}} y$
Since $x_1 \preccurlyeq x_2$ and $x_1 \ne x_2$, the term $\map {U_{n+1}} {x_1}$ is part of the union.
Consequently, $y_2 \notin \map {U_{n+1}} {x_1}$.
This directly contradicts our deduction that $y_2 \in \map {U_{n+1}} {x_1}$.

Therefore, our assumption that $\map {V_{n+2}} z$ intersects two distinct elements of $\AA_n$ must be false.
Thus, for every $z \in X$, there is a set (specifically $\map {V_{n+2}} z$) which intersects at most one element of $\AA_n$.
By the definition of a discrete set of subsets in this context, $\AA_n$ is a discrete set of subsets.
$\blacksquare$
